title: Steering Diffusion Models to Rare Events with Sequential Monte Carlo

paper.title: Steering Diffusion Models to Rare Events with Sequential Monte Carlo
paper.abstract: Abstract Diffusion models are increasingly used as surrogates for expensive simulators in weather prediction, molecular dynamics, and materials design. In these models, computing the probability p 0 ​ [ E ] p_{0}[E] of an event E E is difficult, especially when the event of interest is rare . A stable estimate using Monte Carlo becomes computationally intractable, requiring a growing sample size ∝ 1 / p 0 ​ [ E ] \propto\!1/p_{0}[E] to compensate for an increasing rarity. In this paper, we present D iffusion I mportance Sampling of R are E vents or DireSMC , a sequential Monte Carlo scheme that guides a population of weighted samples towards the rare event, giving access not only to samples but also to a calibrated estimate of its probability. We set up our guidance using an analytical relaxation of the event set, allowing the method to easily extend to a wide range of user-defined rare events. We validate our method on a toy problem with analytical solutions and on a score-based climate emulator, where we obtain accurate rare-event probabilities on a range of rarities from 10 − 3 10^{-3} to 10 − 5 10^{-5} , achieving net speed-ups of 9 × 9\times to 1413 × 1413\times over Monte Carlo.

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text: Score-based diffusion models ( Song et al., 2021b ) are a powerful tool for generative modelling, and have become standard in the quantitative sciences as cheap surrogates for expensive simulators in numerical weather prediction ( Couairon et al., 2026 , Price et al., 2024 ) , molecular simulation ( Abramson et al., 2024 ) and materials design ( Zeni et al., 2025 ) . Trained on data from a distribution p 0 p_{0} , they generate new representative samples by running a denoising process p t p_{t} that anneals from a Gaussian reference p 1 p_{1} down to the data p 0 p_{0} , driven by a learned score ∇ x ​ log ​ p t \nabla_{x}\log p_{t} . Often, scientists are interested in events E E lying in regions where the data distribution assigns little mass p 0 ​ [ E ] p_{0}[E] . Such rare events carry outsized downstream impacts, and arise across a wide range of domains, from the environmental sciences ( Manshausen et al., 2026 , Lancelin et al., 2026 , Peard et al., 2026 ) and bioinformatics ( Xie et al., 2026 ) to finance ( Glasserman and Li, 2005 ) , engineering ( Au and Wang, 2014 ) and autonomous driving ( O'Kelly et al., 2018 ) . Practitioners typically need two things: representative samples of the event, to characterise possible failure modes, and a calibrated estimate of its probability p 0 ​ [ E ] p_{0}[E] , to inform planning and resource allocation ( Kaplan and Garrick, 1981 , Rubino et al., 2009 ) . The simplest approach is to draw N N independent samples and form a Monte Carlo (MC) average to estimate p 0 ​ [ E ] p_{0}[E] , which is difficult precisely because the event is rare. The relative error is 1 / N ​ p 0 ​ [ E ] 1/\sqrt{Np_{0}[E]} , hence stabilising the variance requires N ∝ 1 / p 0 ​ [ E ] N\!\propto\!1/p_{0}[E] samples, which is prohibitively expensive ( Morio et al., 2014 , Rubino et al., 2009 ) . This has motivated a large body of research designed specifically to tackle the poor scaling of standard MC ( Kahn and Harris, 1951 , Morio et al., 2014 , Glasserman and Li, 2005 ) . Diffusion model steering offers a natural method for generating samples from E E without the high costs of simple MC. A reward r 0 r_{0} defines a tilted target π 0 ∝ p 0 ​ e r 0 \pi_{0}\propto p_{0}\,e^{r_{0}} , and inference-time guidance steers a pre-trained sampler towards it. At each denoising step, the gradient of a time-dependent reward r t r_{t} is added, so that the sampler targets π t ∝ p t ​ e r t \pi_{t}\propto p_{t}\,e^{r_{t}} ( Uehara et al., 2025 , Chung et al., 2023 , Song et al., 2023 ) . However, designing a good reward is difficult as the ideal r t r_{t} is often intractable, and any approximations used can guide the sampler towards a different distribution to π 0 \pi_{0} . For rare-event sampling specifically, setting the tilting term e r 0 ≡ 𝟏 E e^{r_{0}}\equiv\mathbf{1}_{E} recovers the rare-event tilted distribution p 0 ( ⋅ | E ) ∝ p 0 𝟏 E p_{0}(\cdot|E)\propto p_{0}\mathbf{1}_{E} that we wish to sample from. However, this reward is a poor object for steering, as its gradient cannot be used to steer particles towards E E . Figure 1: We steer particles ( ∙ \bullet ) from p ref p_{\mathrm{ref}} towards π 0 \pi_{0} , which concentrates mass in the rare-event region of interest, using a guidance drift ∇ x r k {\color[rgb]{1,0,0}\nabla_{x}r_{k}} . Particle size reflects the importance weights accumulated along the trajectory, which are used to resample ( × \times ) and form a rare event estimate, p 0 ​ [ E ] p_{0}[E] . Recent works have attempted to address these problems. The error of using an imperfect reward r t r_{t} can be addressed using sequential Monte Carlo (SMC) by tracking importance weights along the denoising trajectory and resampling particles to focus on high probability regions ( Wu et al., 2023 , He et al., 2026 , Singhal et al., 2025 , Skreta et al., 2025 ) . In diffusion-based molecular simulation, Xie et al. (2026) adapt ideas from Abrams and Bussi (2013) , Shirts and Chodera (2008) to estimate the occupancy of a rare metastable state using collective variables and a sequence of events E i E_{i} converging to E E . Manshausen et al. (2026) instead steer a diffusion model using the probability-flow ODE (PF-ODE) ( Song et al., 2021a ) , and estimate p 0 ​ [ E ] p_{0}[E] using importance sampling. These methods have high compute costs, which become especially problematic in the rare event settings of interest here. Contributions. First , we present DireSMC where we use a sequence of tilted marginals π t \pi_{t} to construct an unbiased sequential Monte Carlo estimator of p 0 ​ [ E ] p_{0}[E] that runs within the denoising process, obtaining both samples and probability estimates. We show that the variance is governed by the quality of our steering rather than the rarity. Second , we show how to design a reward for rare-event simulation, and in particular for threshold-exceedance events E = { x : ϕ ⁡ ( x ) ≥ τ } E\!=\!\{x:\phi(x)\geq\tau\} , giving a smooth surrogate whose look-ahead guidance is closed-form under a Tweedie posterior approximation ( Song et al., 2023 , Chung et al., 2023 ) . Third , we empirically validate on: (1) a Gaussian mixture where ground truth is available and we obtain probability estimates that do not degrade across 10 − 3 10^{-3} – 10 − 5 10^{-5} orders of rarity. (2) a score-based climate emulator, where we draw samples and estimate probabilities of compound hot-and-dry extremes over the region of the 2021 Pacific Northwest heatwave, with net speed-ups of 9 × 9\times to 1413 × 1413\times over Monte Carlo across rarities from 10 − 3 10^{-3} to 10 − 5 10^{-5} .

sections.heading: 3.3 Related work
sections.text: Several works use a pre-trained diffusion sampler to target a tilted distribution without retraining ( Chung et al., 2023 , Song et al., 2023 , Denker et al., 2024 , Berner et al., 2024 , Uehara et al., 2025 ) , but these do not compute probabilities. The weight construction combining diffusion models and SMC samplers ( Skreta et al., 2025 , Wu et al., 2023 , Singhal et al., 2025 , He et al., 2026 ) is common, but our contribution is to apply it to rare-event sampling and probability estimation. In diffusion-based molecular simulations, enhanced rare-event sampling ideas such as metadynamics and umbrella sampling have been adapted ( Xie et al., 2026 ) to estimate the occupancy of a rare metastable state. Both methods track importance weights however, Xie et al. (2026) assemble p 0 ​ [ E ] p_{0}[E] by combining a sequence of events E i E_{i} with MBAR ( Shirts and Chodera, 2008 ) , rather than estimating p 0 ​ [ E ] p_{0}[E] directly. Manshausen et al. (2026) use a score-based climate emulator guidance to generate Tropical Cyclone (TC) events and use importance sampling. An ODE sampler samples the target rare event, followed by two passes of a guided and unguided Probability Flow ODE to estimate its importance weights ( Song et al., 2021b ) . We instead estimate p 0 ​ [ E ] p_{0}[E] by accumulating weights from a single denoising pass and benefit from resampling, which is unavailable to them; see App. J for a comparison.

sections.heading: 4 Experiments
sections.text: We validate DireSMC in two settings: a correlated two-dimensional Gaussian mixture model (GMM) and a pretrained score-based climate emulator. For the GMM, the score and guidance are known analytically so our method may be evaluated in the absence of approximation errors in addition to a learned score, see App. F . The second is a pretrained score-based climate emulator for estimating extreme compound weather events, demonstrating the scalability and applicability of our method. Estimates are evaluated against the sampled law, p ⋆ p^{\star} : closed-form p 0 ​ [ E ] p_{0}[E] for the analytical score or a large MC for the learned score; the same references define the sample-quality metrics. The ratio p ^ 0 ​ [ E ] / p ∗ \hat{p}_{0}[E]/p^{*} measures the bias and the estimator coefficient of variation, CV = Var ​ ( p ^ 0 ​ [ E ] ) / p ⋆ \mathrm{CV}=\sqrt{\mathrm{Var}(\hat{p}_{0}[E])}/\,p^{\star} measures the relative variance computed over independent runs.

Experiments are replicated over 24 24 random seeds and validated against a 200 million MC reference pool (App. G ). Our method recovers the reference exceedance probability for both analytical and learned scores (full per-threshold results and sample-quality metrics in Table 7 , App. G.3 ). For a fixed τ = 10 \tau=10 threshold, Fig. 2 shows that the relative variance decreases as O ⁡ ( 1 / N ) O(1/\sqrt{N}) ( Chatterjee and Diaconis, 2018 ) . Resampling and rejuvenation prevent accumulation of guidance mismatch ( Del Moral et al., 2006 , Del Moral et al., 2012 ) and the CV stays flat across rarities for a fixed N N . DireSMC compares favourably against the importance sampling estimator of Manshausen et al. (2026) . Fig. 2 (left) shows that DireSMC with resampling and MADM leads to lower CV for the same number of particles compared to their method, even though their method requires 3.5 × 3.5\times as many function evaluations as us. In this setting, rejuvenation incurs an additional 1.6 % 1.6\% network calls over the base, which we also discount. On a compute normalised particle budget, all variants of our estimator achieve a lower variance across all rarities as seen in Fig. 2 (cost detailed in App. J and Table 24 ). Additionally, the estimator of Manshausen et al. (2026) assumes that the law induced by an explicit integrator is reversible. However, this often does not hold in practice, leading to a discretisation bias which decreases with step count K K . To isolate the effects of discretisation bias, we ran experiments with the optimal Doob’s transition kernels of Eq. ( 14 ) such that the true p ∗ p^{*} is known and any artefacts due to approximate guidance or score estimates are removed. We also provide the PF-ODE estimator with the true Jacobian trace term, which would otherwise have to be estimated. The results in Fig. 2 (right) show their discretisation bias is significantly larger than DireSMC’s with the bias decreasing with increasing K K (cf. Table 23 ). We acknowledge that our method also incurs a discretisation bias which we characterise below. Ablations. We isolate both the estimator bias and variance introduced by SDE integrators (Euler-Maruyama, SEEDS-1 ( Gonzalez et al., 2023 ) ) and the DDIM ODE integrator ( Song et al., 2021a ) used in Manshausen et al. (2026) . Evaluating with both analytical and learned scores, the discretisation bias decreases approximately as O ⁡ ( 1 / K ) O(1/K) (see Fig. 7 , 9 in App. G.2.2 ). For a fixed K K we find the discretisation bias increases with rarity, highlighting the sensitivity of rare-event probability estimation to small errors. Both SDE integrators track a lower bias compared to DDIM which we postulate is due to the lower overall error in the generation process, see Theorem 3 of Xu et al. (2023) . Moreover, we characterise two sources of errors due to the MADM MCMC kernel ( Lam et al., 2026 ) . It uses the ∇ x ​ log ​ p t = t k \nabla_{x}\log p_{t=t_{k}} to estimate Metropolis Hastings (MH) acceptance ratio, hence targets the continuous-time marginals rather than the law γ k \gamma_{k} induced by the integrator. This introduces an error decaying as O ⁡ ( 1 / K ) O(1/K) to leading order (Fig. 13 ). Additionally, MADM assumes access to a conservative score to compute the ratio which degrades for a learned score network as t → 0 t\rightarrow 0 ( Vuong et al., 2025 ) , see App. G.3.3 for details. Heuristically, we gate rejuvenation to t ∗ > 0 t^{*}>0 to account for this assumption (Table 9 ). Finally, we show that the method translates without modification to interval and multi-constraint events (Table 10 ).

sections.heading: 4.2 Generating heatwaves with pre-trained climate model emulators
sections.text: Next, we validate on the problem of estimating how the probability of extreme events evolves under a changing climate. The high cost of running physics-based climate models ( Eyring et al., 2016 ) has motivated the practice of training cheap emulators on climate model output ( Watson-Parris et al., 2022 ) . However, as we will show, even with these cost-savings, it can be difficult to generate targeted extreme events without explicit steering. Model. We leverage the pre-trained climate emulator of Bouabid et al. (2026) which is trained on data generated from the MPI-ESM1-2-LR model ( Mauritsen et al., 2019 ) and released as part of the Coupled Model Intercomparison Project Phase 6 (CMIP6) ( Eyring et al., 2016 ) . The emulator generates global monthly-mean fields of near-surface temperature ( tas ), precipitation ( pr ), relative humidity ( hurs ) and wind speed ( sfcWind ), conditioned on the global mean surface temperature anomaly, Δ ​ T \Delta T , against a pre-industrial reference and the month of the year, m m , to capture annual variability 1 1 1 As is common in the climate science research literature, the emulator outputs the change in output variables compared to a pre-industrial reference climate rather than absolute predictions. ; we refer to Bouabid et al. We consider extremes in the temperature and humidity variables averaged within the region R R defined by the bounding box 42 ∘ 42^{\circ} - 52 ∘ 52^{\circ} N latitude and 235 ∘ 235^{\circ} - 245 ∘ 245^{\circ} E longitude, roughly corresponding to the region affected by the 2021 Pacific Northwest (PNW) heatwave ( McKinnon and Simpson, 2022 ) . We use N = 1024 N=1024 particles with K = 200 K=200 discretisation steps using the exponential integrator; error/variance metrics are computed using estimates from 16 seeds. We generate ∼ 10 7 \sim 10^{7} Monte Carlo samples to estimate ground-truth event probabilities. Further model details and hyperparameters are presented in App. H . We select the hyperparameters once from a pilot sweep on the marginal hot and dry τ 1 \tau_{1} experiments (detailed below) and use them for all of our other experiments; proper per-problem tuning would lead to a larger variance reduction. Extreme temperatures. We first verify how accurately DireSMC can estimate the probability of extreme temperatures relative to crude Monte Carlo. Assuming Δ ​ T = 1.5 \Delta T=1.5 K, for three different temperature thresholds τ 1 , τ 2 , τ 3 \tau_{1},\tau_{2},\tau_{3} (exact values in App. H ) we calculate the probability that the average surface temperature in the PNW exceeds a temperature threshold in the month of July. The results in Fig. 3 , (full numbers in Table 15 ) show that our method provides significant improvements compared to standard MC estimates with at least an order of magnitude reduction in variance. For the most extreme event τ 3 \tau_{3} , only 2/16 runs provided a single sample above the threshold; hence MC provides almost no samples with which to characterise the event. Figure 3 demonstrates that the generated guided samples provide physically plausible temperature maps: the maps show more warming over land masses compared to the ocean and spatially coherent warming patterns that are not restricted solely to the target region. Additional results and ablations in App. H . Compound hot and dry extremes. Next we probe whether our method can capture extreme events impacting multiple variables by considering events that are both extremely hot and dry because of their outsized societal impacts ( Fan et al., 2023 , Zscheischler et al., 2017 ) . For these joint events it is important to not just consider the separate marginal probabilities of each variable but also to accurately capture the correlations between variables. To do so, we compute the dependence ratio of the event, defined as d = p 0 [ x > τ tas , x < τ hurs ] / p 0 [ x > τ tas ] p 0 [ x < τ hurs ] d=p_{0}[x>\tau_{\texttt{tas}},x<\tau_{\texttt{hurs}}]\,\big/\,p_{0}[x>\tau_{\texttt{tas}}]\,p_{0}[x<\tau_{\texttt{hurs}}] . If the events are independent the dependence ratio would reduce to d = 1 d=1 , while d > 1 d>1 implies that the two events co-occur. We use the non-factorised form of the reward, Φ ⁡ ( ⋅ ) = Φ 2 ​ ( hurs , tas ) \Phi(\cdot)=\Phi_{2}(\texttt{hurs},\texttt{tas}) , a function of both variables; at the rarest level it reduces the CV fourfold relative to a product of marginal rewards (Table 18 ). This temperature approximately corresponds to p 0 ​ [ E ] ≈ 10 − 4 p_{0}[E]\approx 10^{-4} at 1.2 1.2 K (2021) of warming, mirroring the PNW heatwave ( McKinnon and Simpson, 2022 ) . The event moves from a threshold exceedance probability of ∼ 10 − 6 \sim\!10^{-6} at Δ ​ T = 0 \Delta T=0 to a near-certainty at Δ ​ T = 4 \Delta T=4 K. Our estimator tracks it across all six orders of magnitude without any modification. Fig. 4 reports this probability estimate. This experiment shows that the method can be potentially used for climate attribution; see Van Oldenborgh et al. (2021) for an overview.

sections.heading: 5 Conclusion
sections.text: We have shown that the diffusion sampler builds the same annealing bridge that traditional rare-event samplers build by hand. Using this insight, we present DireSMC and steer the generation process towards a user-defined rare event using a smooth relaxation of the event set, accumulating importance weights and estimating the probability along the way. Empirically, on synthetic examples and a score-based climate emulator, we achieve a net speedup of 9 9 to 1413 × 1413\times over crude Monte Carlo, improving with rarity. We believe that this is of value to the scientific community where there is a growing interest in investigating how well a generative model can capture rare events ( Sun et al., 2025 ) . Limitations & Future Work. The variance of our estimator can be improved through better approximations of Doob’s h -transform e.g. ( Potaptchik et al., 2026 , Denker et al., 2024 , Uehara et al., 2025 ) as well as better reward schedule design ( Syed et al., 2026 ) ; these can be readily plugged in without modification to the algorithm. Our estimates target the discretised, approximate law we sample from, and so carry a reducible discretisation bias and any errors of an approximate score. The rejuvenation kernel used ( Lam et al., 2026 ) assumes a conservative score, which a trained network need not provide; distilling the network into an energy model ( Thornton et al., 2025 ) could be a viable solution. Additionally the MADM kernel also does not target the law γ k \gamma_{k} induced by the numerical integrator, with this mismatch decreasing with the weak-order convergence rate of the integrator. Algorithm 1 is agnostic to the choice of MCMC moves, and any alternatives to MADM can be used.

sections.heading: Appendix C Sequential methods
sections.text: For completeness we provide an overview of classical sequential methods that are used in rare-event simulation, such as annealed importance sampling, splitting and sequential Monte Carlo (SMC). These are methods used to bridge the gap from a tractable reference π K \pi_{K} to the tilted target π 0 \pi_{0} of Eq. ( 5 ) through a sequence of overlapping intermediate distributions ( Neal, 2001 , Kahn and Harris, 1951 , Del Moral et al., 2006 ) . We briefly expand on this and highlight their similarities, but refer the readers to ( Moral, 2004 ) for a full exposition under the Feynman-Kac formulation. Additionally, see ( Naesseth et al., 2019 , Del Moral et al., 2006 ) for details on the SMC machinery. Formally the sequence of distributions defines a path-measure over the space of all trajectories particles can take, but we omit this rigour for brevity. Annealed Importance Sampling (AIS) and Sequential Monte Carlo (SMC) build this path by tempering the reward ( Del Moral et al., 2006 , Neal, 2001 ) . One such sequence of distributions tempers the reward, ( Del Moral et al., 2006 , Neal, 2001 ) , π k ​ ( x ) = 1 Z k ​ p 0 ​ ( x ) ​ e β k ​ r ​ ( x ) , 1 = β 0 > β 1 > ⋯ > β K = 0 . \pi_{k}(x)=\frac{1}{Z_{k}}p_{0}(x)\,e^{\beta_{k}r(x)},\qquad 1=\beta_{0}>\beta_{1}>\cdots>\beta_{K}=0. (180) Rather than targeting the constrained target π 0 \pi_{0} directly, tempering gradually sharpens the reward landscape until the chain converges to the target distribution. Additionally, SMC utilises resampling along the trajectory to prune low-weight particles and multiply those with higher weights ( Doucet et al., 2000 , Del Moral et al., 2006 ) . Multilevel splitting takes another approach, where the sequence is constructed using a sequence of nested rare event sets ( Kahn and Harris, 1951 , Glasserman et al., 1999 ) . Taking the canonical example of threshold exceedance, for a strictly decreasing ladder τ 0 = τ > τ 1 > ⋯ > τ K \tau_{0}=\tau>\tau_{1}>\dots>\tau_{K} , the event set is defined as E k = { x : ϕ ⁡ ( x ) ≥ τ k } E_{k}=\{x:\phi(x)\geq\tau_{k}\} . The sequence is defined to be, E 0 = E ⊂ E 1 ⊂ ⋯ ⊂ E K , π k ( x ) = 1 Z k , τ p 0 ( x ) 𝟏 { ϕ ( x ) ≥ τ k } , E_{0}=E\subset E_{1}\subset\cdots\subset E_{K},\qquad\pi_{k}(x)=\frac{1}{Z_{k,\tau}}p_{0}(x)\mathbf{1}\{\phi(x)\geq\tau_{k}\}, (181) where E K E_{K} is a region readily accessible from the state space. The aim of splitting is to estimate the rare event probability at the final τ \tau , i.e. Z 0 , τ = ∫ p 0 ( x ) 1 { ϕ ( x ) ≥ τ 0 } d x = p 0 [ E ] Z_{0,\tau}=\int p_{0}(x)\,\mathbf{1}\{\phi(x)\geq\tau_{0}\}\,dx=p_{0}[E] . We show that all of these methods compute this in the same way. All methods work by transporting particles along the sequence, SMC and splitting additionally resample particles to focus computation on high-weight trajectories (i.e. trajectories that particles undertake that are more likely under the possible sequence of trajectories they could have taken) ( Del Moral et al., 2006 , Glasserman et al., 1999 , Kahn and Harris, 1951 ) . Intuitively, multilevel splitting is a form of SMC/AIS with a hard indicator function replacing a smoothed distribution and the schemes only differ in their construction of their sequences ( Moral, 2004 ) .

sections.heading: Tempering (AIS/SMC)
sections.text: Annealed importance sampling and SMC interpolate by tempering the reward, γ k = p 0 ​ e β k ​ r \gamma_{k}=p_{0}\,e^{\beta_{k}r} , with 1 = β 0 > ⋯ > β K = 0 1=\beta_{0}>\cdots>\beta_{K}=0 , so the incremental weight is given by g k − 1 | k = e ( β k − 1 − β k ) ​ r ​ ( x k ) , Z k − 1 Z k = 𝔼 π k ​ [ e ( β k − 1 − β k ) ​ r ] . g_{k-1\mid k}=e^{(\beta_{k-1}-\beta_{k})\,r(x_{k})},\qquad\frac{Z_{k-1}}{Z_{k}}=\mathbb{E}_{\pi_{k}}\!\big[e^{(\beta_{k-1}-\beta_{k})\,r}\big]. (186) Each normalisation ratio is the average of this factor under the current target. When consecutive temperatures are close, i.e. β k − 1 − β k \beta_{k-1}-\beta_{k} small, the weights stay close to one for all particles and the ratio is estimated reliably. A single large step, by contrast can produce weights spanning many orders of magnitude - collapsing the effective sample size where the final estimate will be dominated by only a few particles that have the largest weights ( Neal, 2001 ) .

sections.heading: Splitting
sections.text: Multilevel splitting interpolates instead with hard indicators, i.e. γ k = p 0 1 { x ∈ E k } \gamma_{k}=p_{0}\,\mathbf{1}\{x\in E_{k}\} , for a shrinking sequence E K ⊃ ⋯ ⊃ E 0 E_{K}\supset\cdots\supset E_{0} . The incremental weight collapses to, g k − 1 | k = p 0 𝟏 { x ∈ E k − 1 } p 0 𝟏 { x ∈ E k } = 𝟏 { x ∈ E k − 1 } , g_{k-1\mid k}=\frac{p_{0}\mathbf{1}\{x\in E_{k-1}\}}{p_{0}\mathbf{1}\{x\in E_{k}\}}=\mathbf{1}\{x\in E_{k-1}\}, (187) for which the ratio of normalisation constant is given by, Z k − 1 Z k = 𝔼 π k [ 𝟏 { x ∈ E k − 1 } ] = Pr [ X ∈ E k − 1 ∣ X ∈ E k ] = : α k , \ \frac{Z_{k-1}}{Z_{k}}=\mathbb{E}_{\pi_{k}}\!\big[\mathbf{1}\{x\in E_{k-1}\}\big]=\Pr[X\in E_{k-1}\mid X\in E_{k}]=:\alpha_{k}, (188) so each ratio is the conditional probability of reaching the next level, estimated by the surviving fraction, α ^ k = N X ∈ E k − 1 / N X ∈ E k \hat{\alpha}_{k}=N_{X\in E_{k-1}}/N_{X\in E_{k}} . Thus the telescoping product of Eq. ( 185 ) for the threshold exceedance given in Eq. ( 181 ) becomes, Z 0 = Z K ∏ k = 1 K α k = Pr [ X > τ K ] ∏ k = 1 K Pr [ X > τ k − 1 ∣ X > τ k ] , Z_{0}=Z_{K}\prod_{k=1}^{K}\alpha_{k}\;=\;\Pr[X>\tau_{K}]\prod_{k=1}^{K}\Pr[X>\tau_{k-1}\mid X>\tau_{k}], (189) This recovers the rare event probability estimate of the multilevel splitting algorithm ( Rubino et al., 2009 , Morio et al., 2014 ) . Both methods estimate the same object via a product of incremental ratios along the bridge where consecutive levels overlap, instead of the single rare-event ratio estimated in one step. This is precisely the failure that accumulating importance weights over the trajectory sidesteps. The diffusion process supplies the sequence of transition kernels and the incremental weights ( Doucet et al., 2022 , Vargas et al., 2023 ) carry their own normalisation avoiding a separate estimate of Z 0 Z_{0} , see Appendix C.3 .

sections.heading: C.3 Why annealing becomes necessary
sections.text: We now motivate why annealing is required and where importance sampling alone is insufficient. Even with exact samples from the tilted target π 0 \pi_{0} of Eq. ( 5 ), taken with r 0 = r 0 , δ r_{0}=r_{0,\delta} or the mollified reward. The naive endpoint (self-normalised) estimator of p 0 ​ [ E ] p_{0}[E] is badly behaved for estimating the normalisation constant, motivating the use of annealing, either via splitting or accumulated importance weights. Given a smooth reward r 0 , δ ​ ( x ) r_{0,\delta}(x) , suppose we can draw exact samples x ∼ π 0 x\sim\pi_{0} from the tilted distribution, π 0 = γ 0 / Z 0 \pi_{0}=\gamma_{0}/Z_{0} with γ 0 = p 0 ​ e r 0 , δ \gamma_{0}=p_{0}e^{r_{0,\delta}} . The rare-event probability under the base distribution p 0 p_{0} can then be written as, p 0 [ E ] = 𝔼 π 0 [ 𝟏 { ϕ ( x ) ≥ τ } p 0 ​ ( x ) π 0 ​ ( x ) ] \displaystyle p_{0}[E]=\mathbb{E}_{\pi_{0}}\!\left[\mathbf{1}\{\phi(x)\geq\tau\}\,\frac{p_{0}(x)}{\pi_{0}(x)}\right] = 𝔼 π 0 [ 𝟏 { ϕ ( x ) ≥ τ } p 0 ​ ( x ) p 0 ​ ( x ) ​ e r 0 , δ ​ ( x ) / Z 0 ] \displaystyle=\mathbb{E}_{\pi_{0}}\!\left[\mathbf{1}\{\phi(x)\geq\tau\}\,\frac{p_{0}(x)}{p_{0}(x)e^{r_{0,\delta}(x)}/Z_{0}}\right] (193) = 𝔼 π 0 [ 𝟏 { ϕ ( x ) ≥ τ } Z 0 e − r 0 , δ ​ ( x ) ] , \displaystyle=\mathbb{E}_{\pi_{0}}\!\left[\mathbf{1}\{\phi(x)\geq\tau\}\,Z_{0}e^{-r_{0,\delta}(x)}\right], where w ⁡ ( x ) := p 0 ​ ( x ) / π 0 ​ ( x ) = Z 0 ​ e − r 0 , δ ​ ( x ) w(x):=p_{0}(x)/\pi_{0}(x)=Z_{0}e^{-r_{0,\delta}(x)} is the importance weight, and the normaliser Z 0 Z_{0} is estimated from the same samples via, 1 Z 0 = 1 Z 0 ​ ∫ p 0 ​ 𝑑 x = 1 Z 0 ​ ∫ p 0 ​ ( x ) ​ e r 0 , δ ​ ( x ) ​ e − r 0 , δ ​ ( x ) = ∫ π 0 ​ e − r 0 , δ ​ ( x ) = 𝔼 π 0 ​ [ e − r 0 , δ ​ ( x ) ] . \frac{1}{Z_{0}}=\frac{1}{Z_{0}}\int{p_{0}}dx=\frac{1}{Z_{0}}\int p_{0}(x)e^{r_{0,\delta}(x)}e^{-r_{0,\delta}(x)}=\int\pi_{0}e^{-r_{0,\delta}(x)}=\mathbb{E}_{\pi_{0}}[e^{-r_{0,\delta}(x)}]. (194) Substituting Eq. ( 194 ) into Eq. ( 193 ) yields the self-normalised importance-sampling (SNIS) estimator ( Owen, 2013 ) , p ^ 0 ​ [ E ] = ∑ i = 1 N 𝟏 { ϕ ( x i ) ≥ τ } e − r 0 , δ ​ ( x i ) ∑ i = 1 N e − r 0 , δ ​ ( x i ) , x i ∼ π 0 ​ ( x ) \hat{p}_{0}[E]\;=\;\frac{\sum_{i=1}^{N}\mathbf{1}\{\phi(x_{i})\geq\tau\}\,e^{-r_{0,\delta}(x_{i})}}{\sum_{i=1}^{N}e^{-r_{0,\delta}(x_{i})}},\qquad x_{i}\sim\pi_{0}(x) (195) The numerator and denominator of ( 195 ) behave very differently. The numerator is only affected by the region that π 0 \pi_{0} approximates well, since the indicator 𝟏 { ϕ ( x ) ≥ τ } \mathbf{1}\{\phi(x)\geq\tau\} provides a “shielding” effect. The denominator, by contrast is an expectation of the normalisation constant Z 0 Z_{0} which is affected by the entire domain of p 0 p_{0} . As the tilt is designed to concentrate on the rare event set, we are effectively using the rare-event tilted distribution π 0 \pi_{0} to estimate a function of p 0 p_{0} . This naturally has a low ESS and yields a high-variance estimate of the normaliser Z 0 Z_{0} . Even given perfect samples from π 0 \pi_{0} we essentially have another “rare-event” expectation in the denominator where no particles of π 0 \pi_{0} fall into the bulk. The denominator integrand w ⁡ ( x ) = p 0 ​ ( x ) π 0 ​ ( x ) = Z 0 ​ e − r 0 , δ ​ ( x ) w(x)=\frac{p_{0}(x)}{\pi_{0}(x)}=Z_{0}e^{-r_{0,\delta}(x)} is largest in the bulk, where p 0 p_{0} holds most of its mass but the tilt π 0 \pi_{0} has almost none, exactly the region π 0 \pi_{0} is designed to avoid . The numerator 𝔼 q ​ [ 𝟏 rare ​ e − r 0 , δ ] \mathbb{E}_{q}[\mathbf{1}_{\text{rare}}e^{-r_{0,\delta}}] stays bounded as it lives where q q samples effectively, whereas the denominator 𝔼 q ​ [ e − r 0 , δ ] \mathbb{E}_{q}[e^{-r_{0,\delta}}] needs exactly the bulk samples that q q avoids. Hence, the ESS for estimating the denominator becomes worse by design and this contributes a high variance estimate of Z 0 Z_{0} ! sections.text: In the case where the path weights are not readily accessible, either because they are not computed or if a large number of discretisation is infeasible, e.g. for a second order numerical integrator. We can fall back to a guided diffusion proposal to build a splitting/annealed probability estimator. In this case, the annealing bridge becomes the nested sequence of event sets defined in Eq. ( 181 ). For the threshold exceedance example given in Sec C , the conditional ratio between adjacent levels is given by, α k = p 0 ​ [ X > τ h ∣ X > τ ℓ ] = p 0 [ X > τ h ∩ X > τ ℓ ] p 0 [ X > τ ℓ ] = p 0 [ X > τ h ] p 0 [ X > τ ℓ ] . \alpha_{k}\;=\;p_{0}[X>\tau_{h}\mid X>\tau_{\ell}]=\frac{p_{0}[X>\tau_{h}\cap X>\tau_{\ell}]}{p_{0}[X>\tau_{\ell}]}=\frac{p_{0}[X>\tau_{h}]}{p_{0}[X>\tau_{\ell}]}. (197) In the denoising-diffusion setting each conditional is sampled by transporting particles from the Gaussian prior to the corresponding target, this means that the probability, Pr [ X > τ h ] \Pr[X>\tau_{h}] is estimated by generating samples from the tilted distribution, p ⁡ ( X ∣ X > τ h ) p(X\mid X>\tau_{h}) , as highlighted in Section 3 . Within this scheme α k \alpha_{k} admits two estimators, depending on whether a single tilt or one tilt per level is used.

sections.heading: Formulation I: single-tilt, two-indicator estimator.
sections.text: Use a single proposal q ℓ q_{\ell} targeting the lower level τ ℓ \tau_{\ell} and estimate both exceedance probabilities from the same particles. With τ ℓ < τ h \tau_{\ell}<\tau_{h} , α k = 𝔼 q ℓ [ 𝟏 { ϕ ( X ) > τ h } e − r ℓ ​ ( X ) ] 𝔼 q ℓ [ 𝟏 { ϕ ( X ) > τ ℓ } e − r ℓ ​ ( X ) ] , \alpha_{k}=\frac{\mathbb{E}_{q_{\ell}}\!\big[\mathbf{1}\{\phi(X)>\tau_{h}\}\,e^{-r_{\ell}(X)}\big]}{\mathbb{E}_{q_{\ell}}\!\big[\mathbf{1}\{\phi(X)>\tau_{\ell}\}\,e^{-r_{\ell}(X)}\big]}, (198) where the shared normaliser Z ℓ Z_{\ell} cancels between numerator and denominator, so it need not be estimated. The denominator is estimated where q ℓ q_{\ell} has mass (it targets τ ℓ \tau_{\ell} ), so it is well-conditioned; the variance is dominated by the numerator, which lives where q ℓ q_{\ell} is sparse ( X > τ h {X>\tau_{h}} ).

sections.heading: Formulation II: two-tilt transitioning.
sections.text: Use one proposal per level, q ℓ ∝ p 0 ​ e r ℓ q_{\ell}\propto p_{0}\,e^{r_{\ell}} and q h ∝ p 0 ​ e r h q_{h}\propto p_{0}\,e^{r_{h}} , and estimate the numerator under q h q_{h} and the denominator under q ℓ q_{\ell} , α k = Z h Z ℓ ​ 𝔼 q h [ 𝟏 { ϕ ( X ) > τ h } e − r h ​ ( X ) ] 𝔼 q ℓ [ 𝟏 { ϕ ( X ) > τ ℓ } e − r ℓ ​ ( X ) ] . \alpha_{k}=\frac{Z_{h}}{Z_{\ell}}\,\frac{\mathbb{E}_{q_{h}}\!\big[\mathbf{1}\{\phi(X)>\tau_{h}\}\,e^{-r_{h}(X)}\big]}{\mathbb{E}_{q_{\ell}}\!\big[\mathbf{1}\{\phi(X)>\tau_{\ell}\}\,e^{-r_{\ell}(X)}\big]}. (199) Each expectation is now evaluated under a tilt matched to its own threshold, so neither term suffers the ESS collapse of Formulation I; the price is that the normalisers no longer cancel and the ratio Z h / Z ℓ Z_{h}/Z_{\ell} must be estimated. Annealing on the output space, i.e. between p 0 ​ e r ℓ → p 0 ​ e r h p_{0}e^{r_{\ell}}\rightarrow p_{0}e^{r_{h}} , we can compute this ratio with the tempering estimator given in Eq. ( 186 ), Z h Z ℓ = 𝔼 q ℓ ​ [ e r h ​ ( X ) − r ℓ ​ ( X ) ] ≈ 1 N ​ ∑ i e r h ​ ( x i ) − r ℓ ​ ( x i ) , x i ∼ q ℓ , \frac{Z_{h}}{Z_{\ell}}=\mathbb{E}_{q_{\ell}}\!\big[e^{\,r_{h}(X)-r_{\ell}(X)}\big]\approx\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i}e^{\,r_{h}(x_{i})-r_{\ell}(x_{i})},\qquad x_{i}\sim q_{\ell}, (200) which is reliable when adjacent tilts overlap. Both formulations require sufficient overlap of the thresholds, the only difference is Formulation I requires overlap between two hard indicators and through the smooth reward difference, r h − r ℓ r_{h}-r_{\ell} , in Formulation II.

sections.heading: Notable Caveats:
sections.text: Evolving directly from p ⁡ ( X ∣ X > τ l ) → p ⁡ ( X ∣ X > τ h ) p(X\mid X>\tau_{l})\rightarrow p(X\mid X>\tau_{h}) is non-trivial without additional training. Unlike traditional splitting, we do not evolve/reuse particles across different thresholds ( Morio et al., 2014 ) , hence the above formulations are not a form of sequential methods. Instead they are a sequence of independent estimators sharing a compute budget. Additionally, any importance weights used assume that within the threshold set by the indicators, samples are well distributed along the tilted distribution. As such both estimators are sensitive to the quality of the guidance. Training based methods could be introduced such as Flow Matching ( Lipman et al., 2023 , Liu et al., 2023 , Albergo and Vanden-Eijnden, 2023 ) or Schrödinger’s Bridges ( Bortoli et al., 2021 , Shi et al., 2023 ) but these remain beyond the scope of this work.

The variance-aware guidance, illustrated in Fig. 5 used in Section 3 is, ∇ x t ​ log ​ 𝔼 p ⁡ ( x 0 ∣ x t ) ​ [ e r 0 , δ ​ ( x 0 ) ] \nabla_{x_{t}}\log\mathbb{E}_{p(x_{0}\mid x_{t})}[e^{r_{0,\delta}(x_{0})}] This appendix derives the closed-form approximation used in our implementation. We consider a general vector-valued constraint ϕ : ℝ d → ℝ m \phi:\mathbb{R}^{d}\to\mathbb{R}^{m} using a Gaussian approximation of the denoising posterior and a local linearisation of ϕ \phi . The scalar affine guidance in Eq. ( 226 ), used for the one-sided threshold-exceedance experiments, is recovered as a special case m = 1 m=1 with a linear- ϕ \phi . We then discuss how interval and compound events are represented by multiple one-sided constraints and the approximation induced when their guidance terms are treated independently. For a multivariate constraint, the smooth reward is a multivariate Gaussian CDF Φ m ( ⋅ ∣ Σ c ) \Phi_{m}(\,\cdot\mid\Sigma_{c}) with constraint covariance Σ c \Sigma_{c} (the smoothing bandwidth; in the scalar case Σ c = δ 2 \Sigma_{c}=\delta^{2} ). The integral is given by, I ⁡ ( x t ) = 𝔼 p ⁡ ( x 0 ∣ x t ) ​ [ Φ m ​ ( ϕ ⁡ ( x 0 ) − τ | Σ c ) ] . I(x_{t})\;=\;\mathbb{E}_{p(x_{0}\mid x_{t})}\!\left[\Phi_{m}\big(\phi(x_{0})-\tau\,\big|\,\Sigma_{c}\big)\right]. (220)

sections.text: Linearising the constraint about the Tweedie mean, ϕ ⁡ ( x 0 ) ≈ ϕ ⁡ ( x ^ 0 | t ) + J ϕ ​ ( x ^ 0 | t ) ​ ( x 0 − x ^ 0 | t ) , J ϕ ​ ( x ^ 0 | t ) = ∇ x 0 ϕ | x ^ 0 | t ∈ ℝ m × d , \phi(x_{0})\;\approx\;\phi(\hat{x}_{0|t})+J_{\phi}(\hat{x}_{0|t})\,(x_{0}-\hat{x}_{0|t}),\qquad J_{\phi}(\hat{x}_{0|t})=\nabla_{x_{0}}\phi\big|_{\hat{x}_{0|t}}\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times d}, (222) makes the integrand a Gaussian convolved with a Gaussian CDF, which integrates in closed form to a single CDF with the two covariances added ( Rasmussen and Williams, 2006 ) , I ⁡ ( x t ) ≈ Φ m ​ ( ϕ ⁡ ( x ^ 0 | t ) − τ | Σ c + J ϕ ​ ( x ^ 0 | t ) ​ Σ t ​ J ϕ ​ ( x ^ 0 | t ) ⊤ ) . (223) The posterior covariance Σ t \Sigma_{t} is thus pushed through the constraint Jacobian and inflates the effective observation variance.

sections.heading: Appendix F The correlated 2D GMM benchmark
sections.text: Figure 6: Base distribution p 0 ​ ( x ) p_{0}(x) of the correlated 2D GMM (log-density, so all modes are visible) with the analytic x 1 x_{1} and x 2 x_{2} marginals. The two right-hand modes ( i = 5 , 6 i=5,6 ) form the tilted “X” of opposite-sign correlation that gives the rare set a bi-modal conditional. This appendix specifies the synthetic benchmark used in our 2D experiments and collects the closed-form quantities it admits: the base density, the normalisation constant Z 0 , δ Z_{0,\delta} of the soft tilt, the exact exceedance probability p 0 ​ [ E ] p_{0}[E] , and the exact Doob guidance ∇ x r t ⋆ = ∇ x ​ log ​ G t \nabla_{x}r^{\star}_{t}=\nabla_{x}\log G_{t} ( Dai Pra, 1991 , Denker et al., 2024 ) . All of these are available in closed form precisely because the GMM prior is conjugate to both the Gaussian forward kernel and the Gaussian-CDF reward, which lets us isolate the behaviour of the estimator from score- and reward-approximation error ( Rasmussen and Williams, 2006 ) .

sections.heading: Base distribution.
sections.text: The data distribution is a M = 7 M=7 -component Gaussian mixture in ℝ 2 \mathbb{R}^{2} , p 0 ​ ( x ) = ∑ i = 1 M w i ​ 𝒩 ​ ( x , μ i , Σ i ) , ∑ i w i = 1 , p_{0}(x)\;=\;\sum_{i=1}^{M}w_{i}\,\mathcal{N}(x;\,\mu_{i},\Sigma_{i}),\qquad\sum_{i}w_{i}=1, (232) where w i w_{i} ( i = 1 , … , M i=1,\dots,M ) denote the mixture weights. The parameters are given in Table 4 . The four “bulk” modes carry most of the mass near the origin; the three right-hand modes are pushed out towards large x 1 x_{1} and given strong off-diagonal covariance ( ρ ≈ ± 0.85 \rho\approx\pm 0.85 ) of opposite sign. sections.heading: The learned score.
sections.text: The learned score for the correlated 7-component GMM of Table 4 , is a velocity prediction MLP trained under the linear VP schedule ( Song et al., 2021b ) . The network takes ( x , emb ⁡ ( t ) ) ∈ ℝ 2 + 128 (x,\mathrm{emb}(t))\in\mathbb{R}^{2+128} , where t t is embedded using a sinusoidal time embedding through 6 layers (hidden width 512, SiLU ( Elfwing et al., 2018 ) ; 1.1 1.1 M parameters) to a two-dimensional output. Targets are v = α t ​ ε − σ ¯ t ​ x 0 v=\alpha_{t}\,\varepsilon-\bar{\sigma}_{t}\,x_{0} with x t = α t ​ x 0 + σ ¯ t ​ ε x_{t}=\alpha_{t}x_{0}+\bar{\sigma}_{t}\varepsilon ; the score used by the sampler is recovered as s θ ( x , t ) = − ε ^ / σ ¯ t s_{\theta}(x,t)=-\hat{\varepsilon}/\bar{\sigma}_{t} with ε ^ = σ ¯ t ​ x + α t ​ v θ ​ ( x , t ) \hat{\varepsilon}=\bar{\sigma}_{t}x+\alpha_{t}v_{\theta}(x,t) . The loss is the per-sample v v -MSE under min-SNR- γ \gamma weighting with γ = 5 \gamma=5 and the weights given by w ⁡ ( t ) = min ⁡ ( SNR ⁡ ( t ) , γ ) / ( SNR ⁡ ( t ) + 1 ) w(t)=\min(\mathrm{SNR}(t),\gamma)/(\mathrm{SNR}(t){+}1) of ( Hang et al., 2023 ) , with t ∼ 𝒰 ⁡ [ 0.01 , 0.99 ] t\sim\mathcal{U}[0.01,0.99] . Training draws fresh exact GMM samples every step: 40,000 steps at batch 4096 with AdamW ( Kingma and Ba, 2014 , Loshchilov and Hutter, 2019 ) (learning rate 2 × 10 − 4 2\times 10^{-4} , weight decay 10 − 4 10^{-4} ), 1,000-step linear warm-up followed by cosine decay, gradient clipping at 1.0 1.0 , and an exponential moving average of the weights (decay 0.999 0.999 ); the EMA weights are used for evaluation. The tempering ladder. Our guidance ladder used through the experiment is λ ⁡ ( t ) = 1 − ( t / t on ) 2 \lambda(t)=1-(t/t_{\rm on})^{2} for t < t on = 0.9 t<t_{\rm on}=0.9 in the case of rejuvenation and λ t ≡ 1 \lambda_{t}\equiv 1 without it, see App. G.5 . sections.heading: G.2 Sources of Bias
sections.text: We begin by discussing the two main contributing factors that bias our estimate against the true p 0 ​ [ E ] p_{0}[E] , followed by additional results. Neither bias is an error of the estimator, and the path-weighted estimator remains unbiased exactly for the law we sample from. The two primary sources are the learning process where the score is approximated poorly (Appendix G.2.1 ) and when the discretised law we sample from differs from the continuous law (Appendix G.2.2 ). We separate and isolate each to study their contributions to the final estimate.

sections.heading: G.2.2 The discretised law: grid and integrator
sections.text: Alongside the bias due to the score estimate, which in the general case cannot be estimated, our discretisation itself induces a distinct, reducible form of bias. Let ℙ \mathbb{P} be the continuous path measure defined by the diffusion process, and ℙ k {\mathbb{P}}_{k} bethe discretised law that we simulate. Our estimator is unbiased for the discrete law that we compute weights for under any guidance ( Del Moral et al., 2006 ) . Hence any gap that remains is a property of the base chain and the integrator alone. This section first measures this gap for two first order integrators and whether the choice of integrator reduces it at a fixed K K .

sections.heading: Setup.
sections.text: Exact Doob guidance (i.e. ∇ x r t ∗ ​ ( x ) \nabla_{x}r_{t}^{*}(x) ), with resampling turned off, so neither guidance error nor adaptive resampling contributes and the residual is resolved above seed noise. We compare the Euler-Maruyama (EM) integrator against the first order exponential SDE solver of ( Gonzalez et al., 2023 ) which we denote as SEEDS-1. Both are explicit one-step schemes of first order. The only difference is that SEEDS-1 treats the integration of the reverse SDE as a semi-linear integral, separating the linear and non-linear parts of the score, and integrating the linear and the noise term exactly, whereas EM approximates it to first order, see ( Gonzalez et al., 2023 , Milstein and Tretyakov, 2004 , Pfarr et al., 2026 ) for more details. Alongside the integrator, the placement of the grid itself is a design choice: we run the sweep on a grid uniform in t t and on a grid uniform in the half-log Signal-to-Noise ratio ℓ t = log ⁡ ( α t / σ ¯ t ) \ell_{t}=\log(\alpha_{t}/\bar{\sigma}_{t}) of App. D.1 , the integrator’s own time variable. sections.heading: The 1 / K 1/K law.
sections.text: Both integrators are one-step schemes of weak order one ( Milstein and Tretyakov, 2004 ) , for which the weak-error admits the expansion c 1 / K + O ⁡ ( 1 / K 2 ) c_{1}/K+O(1/K^{2}) with c 1 c_{1} independent of the step size ( Talay and Tubaro, 1990 , Milstein and Tretyakov, 2004 ) . While this holds for smooth test functions, it does not automatically hold for the indicator 𝟏 E \mathbf{1}_{E} . We therefore fit the form using ordinary least-squares instead of invoking it directly as a theorem. Fitting the coefficient c 1 c_{1} , weighted by the per-K standard errors s k s_{k} , c ^ 1 = ∑ k b k ​ K k − 1 ​ s k − 2 ∑ k K k − 2 ​ s k − 2 , \hat{c}_{1}=\frac{\sum_{k}b_{k}K_{k}^{-1}s_{k}^{-2}}{\sum_{k}K_{k}^{-2}s_{k}^{-2}}, (247) restricted to K ≥ 30 K\geq 30 , since K = 10 K=10 - 20 20 sits outside the asymptotic regime. On the uniform- t t grid the fits are c ^ 1 = + 7.27 \hat{c}_{1}=+7.27 for Euler-Maruyama against − 4.41 -4.41 for SEEDS-1, with largest residuals of 1.6 1.6 and 2.4 2.4 standard errors respectively, so the 1 / K 1/K law holds to within roughly two standard errors over the fitted range. The signs record that the two integrators approach the continuous limit from opposite sides on this grid: EM overestimates and SEEDS-1 underestimates at every K K , and the | EM | / | SEEDS | |\mathrm{EM}|/|\mathrm{SEEDS}| column of Table 6 is the per- K K magnitude comparison. The fitted coefficients track the measurements closely: c ^ 1 = 7.27 \hat{c}_{1}=7.27 predicts + 3.6 % +3.6\% at K = 200 K=200 against a measured + 3.72 % +3.72\% , and + 14.6 % +14.6\% at K = 50 K=50 against + 16.8 % +16.8\% . On the uniform- ℓ \ell grid the EM arm fits similarly ( c ^ 1 = − 4.45 \hat{c}_{1}=-4.45 , largest residual 2.4 2.4 standard errors), but the SEEDS-1 arm changes sign between K = 30 K=30 and K = 50 K=50 : its leading coefficient is small enough that higher-order terms are not negligible over the measured range.

sections.heading: Grid placement.
sections.text: At coarse grids the two placements order the integrators differently. In uniform in t t , SEEDS-1 dominates EM in every K K : the magnitude ratio drops from 4.0 4.0 in K = 10 K=10 towards parity by K ≥ 500 K\geq 500 . For the uniform in the ℓ \ell grid, the order inverts in the coarsest grids K = 10 K=10 and K = 15 K=15 , where we reproduce the result of ( Gonzalez et al., 2023 ) where the performance of the integrator is poor at very small discretisation. We hypothesise that this is because, a uniform Δ ​ ℓ \Delta\ell starves the “middle” of the denoising process, which principled methods for noise-scheduling such as ( Williams et al., 2024 ) place a larger number of discretisation on, see Fig. 4 of ( Williams et al., 2024 ) , which adversely affects the discretised law that we sample. Given that the schedule intimately interplays with Gaussian transition kernel approximation, we leave studying the effects it has on the weight computation for future work. From K ≥ 20 K\geq 20 SEEDS-1 yields a smaller discretisation bias, and the two integrators converge to each other by K = 200 K=200 . We find that in our setting, SEEDS-1 reduces the discretisation bias at lower K K on either grid placement away from the coarsest ℓ \ell -grids, and both integrators are comparable at higher K K ’s. We deploy SEEDS-1 at K = 1000 K=1000 on the uniform- ℓ \ell grid, where both integrators are within 0.2 % 0.2\% of the continuous limit (Table 6 , last row). The exponential integrator is also used in the larger climate experiments.

sections.heading: Both channels improve together.
sections.text: In this experiment, the integrator does not only control the bias but also affects the variance. Across Table 6 the variance diagnostics move with it: on the uniform- t t EM arm the CV falls from 0.338 0.338 to 0.009 0.009 , ESS E \mathrm{ESS}_{E} climbs from 0.032 0.032 to 0.943 0.943 , with the PSIS k ^ \hat{k} dropping below 0.5 0.5 by K = 100 K=100 . The grid placement moves the same diagnostics: at matched K K the ℓ \ell -grid improves ESS E \mathrm{ESS}_{E} and k ^ \hat{k} for both integrators (e.g. at K = 100 K=100 , EM’s ESS E \mathrm{ESS}_{E} is 0.713 0.713 uniform in ℓ \ell against 0.600 0.600 uniform in t t , with k ^ \hat{k} of 0.24 0.24 against 0.40 0.40 ), the coarsest ℓ \ell -grids under SEEDS-1 excepted. These are not two separate effects but one mechanism with two consequences. A finer grid puts the discrete chain closer to the continuous dynamics, which simultaneously shrinks the gap ℙ K − ℙ \mathbb{P}_{K}-\mathbb{P} that the bias measures. As we simulate using the exact Doob’s guidance, this moves the discretised proposal ℚ K \mathbb{Q}^{K} close to the variance minimising Doob’s proposal which helps all other metrics. In a general setting with approximate guidance the dominant source of error is not the discretisation bias but instead the approximation error of Doob’s h-transform, e.g. using DPS. sections.heading: G.3.2 ESS along the trajectory
sections.text: Without resampling the accumulated weight is never reset and the terminal ESS \mathrm{ESS} asymptotically converges to 1 / ( 1 + χ 2 ( ℙ 0 : K ⋆ ∥ ℚ 0 : K ) ) 1/(1+\chi^{2}(\mathbb{P}^{\star}_{0:K}\|\mathbb{Q}_{0:K})) ( Agapiou et al., 2017 ) . Hence for the sampled path, the ESS \mathrm{ESS} measures the gap between the implemented guidance and the exact Doob’s guidance. Figure 11 tracks it along the trajectory for both scores and five thresholds. Two features that are worth noting. The trace is flat at ESS / N = 1 \mathrm{ESS}/N=1 until t ≈ 0.9 t\approx 0.9 , which is the untilted stretch of the denoising time, where the guidance is turned off. After guidance is turned on, the ESS decays monotonically in both learned and analytical arms. The two panels remain close to indistinguishable, highlighting that the profile is set by the guidance geometry rather than the score itself. sections.heading: Benefits of SMC
sections.text: Across, both Tables 8 and 9 , resampling prunes low-weight trajectories and rejuvenation decorrelates duplicated samples. We find that rejuvenation keeps the relative variance constant across rarity for both analytical and learned scores, showing a noticeable decrease in CV if the base estimator is poor ( Del Moral et al., 2006 , Del Moral et al., 2012 ) . (Right) Same value as the left multiplied by ρ \rho for τ > 10 \tau>10 threshold exceedance problem, for different calibrated step sizes ρ \rho , denoted by their average acceptance rate. The shaded band marks the range of gates tested and the dashed line the adopted gate.

sections.heading: Gating the rejuvenation move by noise level
sections.text: For the analytical score, there is no score approximation error, hence the line-integral of the Metropolis-Hastings acceptance ratio is defined exactly up to quadrature error ( Lam et al., 2026 ) . However for a learned score it is approximated by s θ ≈ ∇ x t ​ log ​ p t s_{\theta}\approx\nabla_{x_{t}}\log p_{t} , and any errors in the learning process can lead to a non-conservative score approximation. The left of Fig. 12 , evaluates this via the antisymmetric part of the Jacobian; here we reproduce the findings of ( Lai et al., 2023 , Thornton et al., 2025 ) , where the score network becomes increasingly non-conservative as the denoising time, t → 0 t\rightarrow 0 . A MALA transition kernel requires that M k M_{k} fulfil the Kolmogorov criteria of reversibility. As the Metropolis-Hastings acceptance ratio of MADM ( Lam et al., 2026 ) is estimated by the line-integral of the score, i.e. Eq. ( 253 ); this means the line integral, I ⁡ ( ⋅ ) I(\cdot) must fulfil the cyclic sum (or Stokes’ Theorem), I ⁡ ( b , a ) + I ⁡ ( c , b ) + I ⁡ ( a , c ) = 0 , I(b,a)+I(c,b)+I(a,c)=0, (248) for all triples ( a , b , c ) (a,b,c) . This means that the acceptance ratio of the transition: a → b → c → a a\rightarrow b\rightarrow c\rightarrow a must be equal to 1 for MADM kernel to equate to MALA. A non-conservative score does not fulfil this criterion ( Vuong et al., 2025 ) and hence for a learned score, MADM need not be invariant to π k \pi_{k} . To account for this, we turn off rejuvenation at a specific threshold in time or ℓ t \ell_{t} when the non-conservativity of the score increases. Table 9 ablates different thresholds. At τ = 10 \tau=10 the ungated move reads KS 1.48 / 1.59 1.48/1.59 and EMD 2.10 2.10 against 1.23 / 1.07 / 0.98 1.23/1.07/0.98 when gated at t ≥ 0.30 t\geq 0.30 , and the same ordering holds at τ = 9 \tau=9 ; we therefore adopt the gated rejuvenation for the rest of our examples, selecting the middle of the values we tested, ℓ t ≤ − 0.21 \ell_{t}\leq-0.21 ( t ≥ 0.30 t\geq 0.30 ). At τ = 7 , 8 \tau=7,8 , where the corrector and resampling events were triggered less frequently, the gated and ungated rows coincide within noise, as the ungated version already sits close to the noise floor. Both gated and un-gated arms at τ = 10 \tau=10 read 0.965 0.965 and 0.994 0.994 within 1.3 1.3 standard errors.

sections.heading: Step size selection
sections.text: As the step-size ρ \rho defines the region where a move is proposed, i.e. x ~ − x ∼ 𝒩 ⁡ ( ρ ​ g ​ ( x ) / 2 , ρ ​ I ) \tilde{x}-x\sim\mathcal{N}(\rho g(x)/2,\rho I) of Eq. ( 249 ), a larger ρ \rho leads to, what we hypothesise, a higher exposure to the non-conservative part of the score network, which affects the estimated M k M_{k} further. For a simple visualisation, we plot the proposed step size ρ \rho multiplied by the Frobenius norm of the antisymmetric part of the Jacobian, to the right of Fig 12 . This for various ρ \rho on the τ = 10 \tau=10 threshold exceedance problem of Section 4.1 ; here the step size has been tuned to target a range of acceptance probabilities as is common ( Lam et al., 2026 ) . We elect to take smaller, more conservative steps, tuning ρ \rho to target a 0.72 acceptance. We hypothesise that, for a fixed number of MADM steps and ρ \rho , there is a tradeoff between the total number of MADM steps that rejuvenate duplicated particles and the net error injected into the system by an approximate MH ratio. An adaptive schedule on ρ ⁡ ( t ) \rho(t) or M ⁡ ( t ) M(t) that accounts for these trade-offs could be an interesting direction for future work.

sections.heading: H.1 Setup and model details
sections.text: We use a pretrained score-based diffusion climate emulator that acts as a surrogate for physics-based Earth System Models ( Bouabid et al., 2026 ) (licensed under MIT Licence), trained on large-ensemble runs from the Coupled Model Intercomparison Project (CMIP6) on different climate change (forcing) scenarios ( O’Neill et al., 2016 ) . Our results are based on the MPI-ESM1-2-LR emulator. The model outputs monthly-averaged fields conditioned on the global mean surface temperature anomaly (GMST), which captures global warming against preindustrial warming, and on the month of the year, which captures annual variability. The emulator generates four surface fields jointly across the globe on every draw, listed in Table 12 by their CMIP6 short names. All fields are monthly means and are handled throughout as anomalies against the pre-industrial (piControl) climatology, matching the convention of Table 13 . sections.heading: H.1.1 Implementation Details
sections.text: For all experiments throughout we use K = 200 K=200 discretisation of the exponential integrator in the noise-prediction mode, see App. D and Fig. 15 . We schedule λ ⁡ ( t ) \lambda(t) and δ ⁡ ( t ) \delta(t) for all experiments below. For a VE-schedule, α t ≡ 1 \alpha_{t}\equiv 1 , so the half-log SNR is ℓ t = − log ⁡ σ ¯ t \ell_{t}=-\log\bar{\sigma}_{t} and we specify both schedule in σ ¯ t \bar{\sigma}_{t} : piecewise linear in λ \lambda and δ t \delta_{t} is interpolated log-linearly between two endpoints. Similar to GMM example, we turn guidance, i.e. λ ⁡ ( t ) ≡ 0 \lambda(t)\equiv 0 off for the first 15% ( OPEN σ ¯ > 40 ) \bar{\sigma}>40) of the denoising process to account for any approximation errors in x ^ 0 | t \hat{x}_{0|t} , converging to λ ⁡ ( σ ¯ ) → 1 \lambda(\bar{\sigma})\rightarrow 1 after adding a lambda overshoot at a maximum of 1.25. δ ⁡ ( t ) \delta(t) is held at 0.5 until σ ¯ = 0.3 \bar{\sigma}=0.3 SD and sharpens to 0.01 by σ ¯ = 0.03 \bar{\sigma}=0.03 SD, where SD is the standard deviation of each observable approximated by the same method as the Π \Pi GDM mentioned in App B . We decrease δ \delta towards the end of the denoising process to reduce the variance of our estimator due to mismatch in the generated π 0 \pi_{0} . For simplicity, we do not anneal τ ⁡ ( σ ¯ ) \tau(\bar{\sigma}) . Correctness of our method is independent of these choices, so they are selected for variance alone. We set them empirically on the p ∗ ≈ 10 − 3 p^{*}\approx 10^{-3} rarity, PNW marginal hot and dry threshold exceedance problems using a pilot sweep at the same setup as described above. We provide an ablation of the values we tested below (Table 22 ), but adopt the same hyper-parameters for all experiments, with N = 1024 N=1024 , K = 200 K=200 and 16 16 seeds throughout, see Table 14 . sections.heading: H.2.1 Selection and rejuvenation
sections.text: Similar to Appendix G.3.3 , we ablate the effect of resampling and rejuvenation on the hot and dry threshold exceedance events and the joint hot-and-dry event that we report the net speed-up on. This is because while resampling does not cost extra wall clock time, rejuvenation does. We evaluate whether the reduction in CV justifies the added computation cost. For this, we use a fixed M = 5 M=5 MADM steps using 2 degrees of quadrature. Additionally, we cache the estimate of log ⁡ Γ π \log\Gamma_{\pi} in Eq. ( 254 ) for either the current x x or proposal x ~ \tilde{x} so that it may be reused between moves. For the same reasons as highlighted in Appendix G , we set the acceptance target at 0.72 0.72 and gate the rejuvenation move to run only at noise levels σ ¯ ≥ 0.30 \bar{\sigma}\geq 0.30 . Table 16 captures this ablation. We report the CV which is the spread of the estimated p ^ \hat{p} across 16 seeds; k ^ \hat{k} is the generalised-Pareto shape parameter of the importance weights, fitted with the top 96 ( min ⁡ ( 0.2 ​ N , 3 ​ N ) \min(0.2N,3\sqrt{N}) ) ( Vehtari et al., 2024 ) , within a run, reported as the median over seeds. We find that without resampling the median k ^ \hat{k} exceeds 0.5 0.5 (no finite second moment) in seven of the nine cells. This suggests that the weights are very heavy-tailed and the convergence of the no-resampling estimator is slow to converge, with an accompanying CV that is optimistic. Resampling lowers the CV in eight of the nine cells; the exception, dry at 10 − 4 10^{-4} , comes from a single collapsed run in which one lineage takes over the crossing particles (seed 12, p ^ / p ⋆ = 1.72 \hat{p}/p^{\star}=1.72 with 5 effective families); without it the CV is 0.124 0.124 . Rejuvenation does not change the CV consistently: it is lower for hot at 10 − 5 10^{-5} and for dry at 10 − 4 10^{-4} , where no rejuvenated run collapses, and higher in the other seven cells, by at most 27 % 27\% . Differences of this size are within the sampling error of a CV estimated from 16 seeds. W 1 W_{1} is the weighted Wasserstein-1 distance of the quantity of interest ϕ ⁡ ( ⋅ ) \phi(\cdot) between the generated samples and the Monte Carlo reference, reported against a null floor. All variants report a similar W 1 W_{1} and there is no discernible issue with any. However, it is worth noting that rejuvenation adds ∼ 1.1 {\sim}1.1 – 1.25 × 1.25\times wall-clock time compared to resampling alone, hence there is a trade-off between a larger N N versus more rejuvenation steps at finite compute budget. In the experiments below, unless stated otherwise we run with zero rejuvenation steps. sections.heading: H.2.4 Factorised versus multivariate guidance
sections.text: We ablate the two reward variants - factorised (Eq. ( 229 )) and joint (Eq. ( 223 )) of the compound weather event of Section 4.2 . Across rarities, we compute the guidance based on a factorised reward (i.e. a product of two independent 1-dimensional CDFs) and its correlated Φ 2 \Phi_{2} variant. Both variants yield a different guidance drift as well as look-ahead reward r 0 , δ r_{0,\delta} . Additionally, for the Gaussian surrogate of p ⁡ ( x 0 | x t ) ≈ N ⁡ ( x ^ 0 | t , Σ ) p(x_{0}|x_{t})\approx N(\hat{x}_{0|t},\Sigma) , where x ^ 0 | t \hat{x}_{0|t} is Tweedie’s estimate, we replace the isotropic Σ \Sigma approximation of ( Song et al., 2023 ) , with a JVP estimate of σ 2 ​ A T ​ J ​ A \sigma^{2}A^{T}JA , where A A is defined by the linear function, J J is the Jacobian of the network and σ 2 \sigma^{2} is the current noise level (Appendix E.1 ). The joint estimator costs roughly 1.64 × 1.64\times wall-clock time (Appendix H.4 ) of the factorised but yields a lower variance of p 0 ​ [ E ] p_{0}[E] at the rarest level, which we discuss below. sections.heading: H.4 Computational cost
sections.text: We measure the net-speed-up of the path-weighted estimator by comparing the net wall-clock time required for each example in Table 21 . We compare our results against the number of N M ​ C N_{MC} samples required to form a Monte Carlo estimate at equal-CV, discounted by the added cost of computing the guidance. An unguided draw is one denoiser call per step ( 0.151 0.151 s per sample at K = 200 K=200 ); the production sampler measures 4.7 × 4.7\times that per sample for a univariate or factorised reward (marginal threshold exceedances and multivariate exceedance under uncorrelated reward), and the correlated variant of the reward measures a larger 7.7 × 7.7\times . In general, any m m -coupled reward requires m m vector Jacobian product calls per denoising step, which contributes a linearly growing computational cost to the wall-clock time. sections.heading: Appendix J Related Works Extended
sections.text: We compare our method for generating the rare event probabilities against the method introduced in ( Manshausen et al., 2026 ) . Both methods guide a pre-trained diffusion model towards the extremes, and reweight the resulting samples to estimate p 0 ​ [ E ] p_{0}[E] under the model density p θ p_{\theta} . The methods differ at the integrator. The method of ( Manshausen et al., 2026 ) samples with an ODE and estimates the rare-event probability using the Probability Flow ODE (PF-ODE) ( Song et al., 2021b ) for both unguided and guided processes, which allows them to weight each sample by its exact terminal likelihood. We sample with a reverse SDE and weight each trajectory by the Girsanov density of the guided path measure, computed against the unguided process. Neither object is available to the other: a stochastic integrator has no PF-ODE likelihood, and a deterministic flow induces path measures that are mutually singular, so Girsanov’s theorem is not available. Resampling mid-trajectory is only available to the path-weights formulation as a terminal-only weight defines no intermediate targets to resample against. During the denoising process, we measure how far the sampled trajectory ℚ \mathbb{Q} deviates from one defined by the tilted process ℙ r 0 , δ \mathbb{P}_{r_{0,\delta}} , and adaptively resample within a Sequential Monte Carlo scheme. Under the operating guidance of ( Manshausen et al., 2026 ) , this yields us a far larger fraction of particles from the rare-event set E E .

We too need large K K for this to be satisfied. In the absence of p 0 p_{0} and D map D_{\mathrm{map}} , our condition is trivially satisfied, whereas ( Manshausen et al., 2026 ) requires ℰ 0 = ℰ γ \mathcal{E}_{0}=\mathcal{E}_{\gamma} or the cancellation of individual biases.

sections.heading: J.1.1 Empirical results
sections.text: As the laws induced by the discretised ODE and SDE integrators need not coincide generally for a learned score, see Deveney et al. (2025) , we evaluate the bias using analytical scores where the true rare-event probability p 0 ​ [ E ] p_{0}[E] is known without any discretisation bias. We compare these methods using the 2D GMM threshold exceedance problem at τ = 10 \tau=10 . As both methods use first order integrators, we use the exponential integrator for both ODE and SDE variants with analytical scores and Doob’s guidance on the tested equal ℓ \ell discretisation (see App. G.2.2 ). In the ODE setting of ( Manshausen et al., 2026 ) , this is equivalent to the DDIM ( Song et al., 2021a , Lu et al., 2022 , Gonzalez et al., 2023 ) integrator, but under the EDM’s parametrisation ( Karras et al., 2022 ) this corresponds to the Euler integrator used in ( Manshausen et al., 2026 ) . Additionally, we clip the guidance to ensure that the crossing fraction remains 10 % 10\% for both methods (under no resampling) which mirrors the operational regime of ( Manshausen et al., 2026 ) . We calibrate the clipping for both methods at each K K separately.
